title: Intersections and angles of lines and planes
summary: Lines and planes can meet at a point, along a line, or not at all. Solving their equations together tells you which: the system has one solution, infinitely many or none. Their angles come from scalar products of direction and [[normal-vector|normal]] vectors.

goals.text: Find where a line meets a plane, or show that it is parallel to the plane or lies in it.
Find the [[line-of-intersection|line of intersection]] of two planes, and recognise parallel planes.
Solve the equations of three planes as a linear system, and describe the arrangement each kind of solution shows.
Find the angle a line makes with a plane.
Find the angle between two planes, and tell when they are perpendicular.

synonyms: angle between a line and a plane

before.prompt: Which vector is normal to the plane $4x - y + 3z = 10$?
before.hint: The coefficients of $x$, $y$ and $z$ in a Cartesian equation give a normal.
before.explain: In $ax + by + cz = d$ the normal is $(a, b, c)$, signs included. The $10$ only fixes where the plane sits. Revise it in {{lesson:3.17}}.

before.hint: Use the booklet's components, with care over the middle one.
before.explain: The components are $2 \times 3 - 0 \times 1 = 6$, $0 \times 0 - 1 \times 3 = -3$ and $1 \times 1 - 2 \times 0 = 1$. Revise it in {{lesson:3.16}}.

before.prompt: Row reduction of a system in $x$, $y$ and $z$ gives $\left(\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 4 \end{array}\right)$. Find $x$.
before.hint: Start from the bottom row, which says $2z = 4$.
before.explain: $z = 2$. Then $y + 3z = 7$ gives $y = 1$, and $x + 2y - z = 3$ gives $x = 3 - 2 + 2 = 3$. Revise it in {{lesson:1.16}}.

sections.heading: Where a line meets a plane

blocks.text: In {{lesson:3.15}} two lines meeting meant solving for two parameters. A line meeting a plane needs only one. A point of the line that is also on the plane must satisfy the plane's equation.
1. Write the general point of the line, using its [[parametric-equations-of-a-line|parametric equations]].
2. Substitute it into the plane's Cartesian equation, $ax + by + cz = d$.
3. Solve the equation for $\lambda$, then put $\lambda$ back into the line to get the point.
The equation in step 2 is linear in $\lambda$. So it has one solution, none, or every $\lambda$ works.

blocks.alt: Three panels, each with a flat plane drawn as a shaded parallelogram. Left: a line passes down through the plane, crossing it at one marked point, and continues dashed below it. Middle: a line runs above the plane at a constant height, shown by two equal dotted drops to the plane, so it never meets it. Right: a line is drawn lying flat on the plane.
blocks.caption: One solution for $\lambda$, no solution, or every $\lambda$.

blocks.statement: Substituting gives an equation $p\lambda = q$. If $p \neq 0$, the line meets the plane at one point. If $p = 0$ and $q \neq 0$, it is parallel to the plane and never meets it. If $p = q = 0$, it lies in the plane.
blocks.why: $p = \boldsymbol{b} \cdot \boldsymbol{n}$, where $\boldsymbol{n}$ is the [[normal-vector|normal]]. So $p = 0$ exactly when the direction is perpendicular to the normal.

blocks.question: Find the coordinates of the point where the line $\boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}$ meets the plane $x + 2y - z = 6$.
steps: Write the general point of the line: $x = 2 + \lambda$, $y = -1 + 3\lambda$, $z = 3 - 2\lambda$.
Substitute into the plane: $(2 + \lambda) + 2(-1 + 3\lambda) - (3 - 2\lambda) = 6$.
Expand and collect: $2 + \lambda - 2 + 6\lambda - 3 + 2\lambda = 6$, so $9\lambda - 3 = 6$ and $\lambda = 1$.
Put $\lambda = 1$ into the line: $x = 3$, $y = 2$, $z = 1$.
Check in the plane: $3 + 2(2) - 1 = 6$. It works.

blocks.text: With an unknown constant, choose it to make the coefficient of $\lambda$, or the right-hand side, zero.

blocks.question: The line $L$ has equation $\boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\4\end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\k\end{pmatrix}$, and the plane $\Pi$ has equation $3x + 4y - z = d$, where $k, d \in \mathbb{R}$. Find $k$ and $d$ so that $L$ lies in $\Pi$.
steps: Substitute the general point $(1 + 2\lambda,\ -\lambda,\ 4 + k\lambda)$ into $\Pi$: $3(1 + 2\lambda) + 4(-\lambda) - (4 + k\lambda) = d$.
Collect the $\lambda$ terms: $(6 - 4 - k)\lambda + 3 - 4 = d$, that is $(2 - k)\lambda = d + 1$.
$L$ lies in $\Pi$ only if this holds for every $\lambda$. So the coefficient must be zero: $k = 2$.
Then the equation reads $0 = d + 1$, true only when $d = -1$. Any other $d$ makes $L$ parallel to $\Pi$ without meeting it.

blocks.text: Testing a single point. A point on the plane proves they meet; the whole line is in the plane only if $\boldsymbol{b} \cdot \boldsymbol{n} = 0$ too.

blocks.prompt: Find the point where the line $\boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix} + \mu\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}$ meets the plane $2x + y + z = 7$.
blocks.hint: Substitute $x = \mu$, $y = 1 - \mu$ and $z = -2 + 3\mu$ into the plane's equation.

blocks.prompt: How does the line $\boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\0\end{pmatrix} + t\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ sit relative to the plane $x - 2y + z = -3$?
blocks.hint: Substitute the general point into the plane. What happens to $t$?

options.text: It is parallel and never meets it.
It meets it at exactly one point.

blocks.explain: $(1 + 3t) - 2(2 + t) - t = -3$ simplifies to $-3 = -3$, true for every $t$. The $t$ terms cancel because $\boldsymbol{b} \cdot \boldsymbol{n} = 3 - 2 - 1 = 0$.

blocks.text: Two pages of an open book meet along the spine, a straight line. Two planes do the same unless they are parallel. Two equations in three unknowns usually leave one unknown free ({{lesson:1.16}}).

blocks.statement: The [[line-of-intersection|line of intersection]] of two non-parallel planes is the set of points that satisfy both of their equations.
blocks.plain: The crease where two flat sheets meet.

blocks.statement: Two planes with non-parallel [[normal-vector|normals]] meet in a line. If their normals are parallel, the planes are either parallel and never meet, or they are the same plane.
blocks.why: Scale one equation so the left sides match. Equal right sides then give the same plane; different ones give no common point.

blocks.text: To find the line, remove one unknown between the equations. Let another equal $\lambda$ and write the rest in terms of it.

blocks.question: Find a vector equation of the line where the planes $x + y + 2z = 5$ and $2x - y + z = 1$ meet.
steps: The normals $(1, 1, 2)$ and $(2, -1, 1)$ are not multiples of each other, so the planes meet in a line.
Add the equations to remove $y$: $3x + 3z = 6$, so $x = 2 - z$.
Let $z = \lambda$. Then $x = 2 - \lambda$.
From the first equation, $y = 5 - x - 2z = 5 - (2 - \lambda) - 2\lambda = 3 - \lambda$.

So every point of the line is $(2 - \lambda,\ 3 - \lambda,\ \lambda)$. Check in the second plane: $2(2 - \lambda) - (3 - \lambda) + \lambda = 4 - 2\lambda - 3 + \lambda + \lambda = 1$ for every $\lambda$.

blocks.text: A second method: the line lies in both planes, so its direction is perpendicular to both normals. The vector product from {{lesson:3.16}} gives such a vector.
Here $\boldsymbol{d}$ is the line's direction. For a point, set $z = 0$ and solve for $x$ and $y$. If $\boldsymbol{d}$ has $z$-component $0$, set $x$ or $y$ to $0$ instead.

blocks.question: The planes $\Pi_{1}$ and $\Pi_{2}$ have equations $3x - 2y + z = 7$ and $x + y - 2z = -1$. Find a vector equation of their line of intersection.
steps: Read off the normals: $\boldsymbol{n}_{1} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{n}_{2} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}$.
Find the direction: $\boldsymbol{n}_{1} \times \boldsymbol{n}_{2} = \begin{pmatrix}(-2)(-2) - (1)(1)\\(1)(1) - (3)(-2)\\(3)(1) - (-2)(1)\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\7\\5\end{pmatrix}$.
Check it is perpendicular to both normals: $3(3) - 2(7) + 1(5) = 0$ and $1(3) + 1(7) - 2(5) = 0$.
Find a point. Set $z = 0$: $3x - 2y = 7$ and $x + y = -1$. The second gives $y = -1 - x$, so $3x + 2 + 2x = 7$, $x = 1$ and $y = -2$.

blocks.text: A sign slip in the vector product's middle component. For $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}$ it is $v_{3}w_{1} - v_{1}w_{3}$. Check your direction against both normals: each scalar product must be $0$.

blocks.prompt: How do the planes $2x - 4y + 6z = 3$ and $-x + 2y - 3z = 5$ meet?
blocks.hint: Compare the normals, then the right-hand sides.

options.text: They are parallel and never meet.

blocks.explain: $(2, -4, 6) = -2(-1, 2, -3)$, so the planes are parallel. Doubling the second equation and changing signs gives $2x - 4y + 6z = -10$, not $3$, so they never meet.

blocks.prompt: Which is a vector equation of the line where the planes $x - y + z = 2$ and $2x + y - z = 7$ meet?
blocks.hint: Adding the equations removes both $y$ and $z$.
blocks.explain: Adding gives $3x = 9$, so $x = 3$ all along the line. Then $y - z = 1$: let $z = \lambda$, so $y = 1 + \lambda$.

blocks.text: Three planes give three equations in $x$, $y$ and $z$: a system like those in {{lesson:1.16}}. Its solutions are the points on all three planes, so the number of solutions shows how the planes are arranged.
Usually they share one point, like the floor and two walls at the corner of a room. If they all pass through one line, like pages turning on a spine, they form a [[sheaf-of-planes|sheaf]].

blocks.statement: Three planes meet at a single point if the system has one solution, and in a line if the solutions need one parameter. With two parameters they are all the same plane. With no solution they share no point.
blocks.why: The solutions of the system are exactly the points that lie on all three planes.

blocks.text: With no solution, check the [[normal-vector|normals]]. If two are parallel, those planes are parallel. If none are, each pair meets in a line, the lines are parallel, and the planes form a triangular prism.

blocks.alt: Four panels, each showing three planes seen end-on, so each plane looks like a straight line. First: three lines through one shared point, labelled common line, infinitely many. Second: three lines crossing in pairs to make a triangle, labelled triangular prism, no solution. Third: two parallel lines cut by a third line, labelled two parallel, no solution. Fourth: three parallel lines, labelled three parallel, no solution.
blocks.caption: Seen end-on, a common line looks like a point. The single-point case can't be drawn end-on.

blocks.text: On Paper 2 the GDC's equation solver finds a single point. Write down the [[augmented-matrix|augmented matrix]] you enter.

blocks.question: The planes $\Pi_{1}$, $\Pi_{2}$ and $\Pi_{3}$ have equations $1.2x - y + 2z = 3.5$, $x + 2y - 0.5z = 4$ and $3x + y + z = 6.8$. Use your calculator to find the coordinates of the point where they meet. Give each coordinate to 3 s.f.
steps: Write down what you enter: $\left(\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1.2 & -1 & 2 & 3.5 \\ 1 & 2 & -0.5 & 4 \\ 3 & 1 & 1 & 6.8 \end{array}\right)$.
The solver gives $x = 0.67777\ldots$, $y = 2.28222\ldots$ and $z = 2.48444\ldots$, a unique solution. So the planes meet at one point.
Check with the unrounded values in $\Pi_{3}$: $3(0.67777\ldots) + 2.28222\ldots + 2.48444\ldots = 6.8$.
Round each to 3 s.f.: the point is $(0.678, 2.28, 2.48)$.

ti84: Choose the simultaneous equation solver, with 3 equations and 3 unknowns (check on your model)
nspire: Calculator page: Menu, Algebra, Solve System of Linear Equations
Number of equations: 3, variables x, y, z, OK (check on your model)
casio: Number of unknowns: 3 (check on your model)

blocks.text: With a parameter, row reduce by hand. The last row's coefficient decides whether there is one point; its right-hand side then decides between a line and no common point.

blocks.question: The planes $\Pi_{1}$, $\Pi_{2}$ and $\Pi_{3}$ have equations $x + y + z = 2$, $x + 2y - z = 1$ and $2x + 3y + kz = m$, where $k, m \in \mathbb{R}$. Find $k$ and $m$ so that the three planes meet in a line.
steps: Clear the first column. $R_{2} - R_{1}$ gives $(0,\ 1,\ -2 \mid -1)$ and $R_{3} - 2R_{1}$ gives $(0,\ 1,\ k - 2 \mid m - 4)$.
The new $R_{3}$ minus the new $R_{2}$ gives $(0,\ 0,\ k \mid m - 3)$, which says $kz = m - 3$.
If $k \neq 0$, then $z = \frac{m - 3}{k}$: one solution, a single point. So a line needs $k = 0$.
With $k = 0$ the row is $(0,\ 0,\ 0 \mid m - 3)$. It is all zeros, giving infinitely many solutions, only when $m = 3$.

Let $z = \lambda$. Row 2 gives $y = -1 + 2\lambda$, and row 1 gives $x = 3 - 3\lambda$. The line is $\boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix}-3\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}$.
If $k = 0$ and $m \neq 3$, there is no solution. No two normals are parallel, so the planes then form a prism.

blocks.text: Making only the coefficient in the last row zero. A row $(0,\ 0,\ 0 \mid c)$ gives a common line only when $c = 0$ too.

blocks.prompt: Row reduction of the equations of three planes gives $\left(\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & -1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array}\right)$. How do the planes meet?
blocks.hint: Read the last row as an equation. How many unknowns are free?

options.text: They meet at a single point.
They have no point in common.
They are all the same plane.

blocks.explain: The last row says $0 = 0$, leaving two equations: one unknown is free, so the planes share a line.

blocks.prompt: The planes $x + 2y - z = 1$, $2x + y + z = 4$ and $x - y + az = 3$ meet in a line for exactly one value of $a$. Find it.
blocks.hint: Row reduce, carrying $a$ along, and look at the last row.
blocks.explain: $R_{2} - 2R_{1}$ gives $(0,\ -3,\ 3 \mid 2)$ and $R_{3} - R_{1}$ gives $(0,\ -3,\ a + 1 \mid 2)$. Subtracting leaves $(0,\ 0,\ a - 2 \mid 0)$, all zeros when $a = 2$.

blocks.prompt: Describe how the planes $x + y + z = 1$, $x - y + 2z = 3$ and $3x + y + 4z = 2$ are arranged.
blocks.hint: Compare the third equation with twice the first plus the second.

options.text: Two of the planes are parallel.
They meet at a single point.

blocks.explain: Twice the first plus the second is $3x + y + 4z = 5$, but the third has $2$ on the right, so no point is on all three. No two normals are parallel: a prism.

sections.heading: Angle between a line and a plane

blocks.text: Shine a light straight down onto a plane, and a line casts a shadow on it. The [[angle-between-line-and-plane|angle between the line and the plane]] is the angle between the line and its shadow, from $0^{\circ}$ to $90^{\circ}$.

The shadow is awkward to find, but the [[normal-vector|normal]] comes straight from the plane's equation. If the line makes angle $\theta$ with the plane, it makes $90^{\circ} - \theta$ with the normal.

blocks.alt: A shaded plane with a point P on it. The normal vector n rises straight up from P. The line L leaves P upwards to the right. A dashed line on the plane runs from P directly below L, labelled projection of L, with a right angle where a dotted drop from L meets it. The angle theta is marked between L and its projection, and the angle 90 degrees minus theta between L and the normal.
blocks.caption: The angle with the plane, $\theta$, and the angle with the normal, $90^{\circ} - \theta$, add to $90^{\circ}$.

blocks.text: The booklet gives the angle between two vectors.
With the line's direction $\boldsymbol{b}$ and the plane's normal $\boldsymbol{n}$, it gives the angle with the normal. Since $\cos(90^{\circ} - \theta) = \sin\theta$, you get a formula to learn.
If $\boldsymbol{n}$ points the other way, the angle with the normal is $90^{\circ} + \theta$ instead, and its cosine is $-\sin\theta$. The modulus removes that sign, so $\theta$ is always acute.

blocks.question: Find the angle between the line $\boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and the plane $2x + y + z = 5$.
steps: Read off the line's direction, $\boldsymbol{b} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}$, and the plane's normal, $\boldsymbol{n} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}$.
Scalar product: $\boldsymbol{b}\cdot\boldsymbol{n} = 1(2) + (-1)(1) + 2(1) = 3$.
Magnitudes: $\lvert\boldsymbol{b}\rvert = \sqrt{1 + 1 + 4} = \sqrt{6}$ and $\lvert\boldsymbol{n}\rvert = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 1} = \sqrt{6}$.
So $\sin\theta = \frac{3}{\sqrt{6}\sqrt{6}} = \frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$.
$\theta$ is acute, so $\theta = 30^{\circ}$. The angle with the normal is $60^{\circ}$, making $90^{\circ}$ in total.

blocks.question: The line $L$ passes through $\mathrm{A}(1, -2, 3)$ and $\mathrm{B}(4, 0, -1)$. Find the acute angle between $L$ and the plane $x - 3y + 2z = 6$. Give your answer in degrees to 3 s.f.
steps: Direction of $L$: $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\-4\end{pmatrix}$. Normal of the plane: $\boldsymbol{n} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\-3\\2\end{pmatrix}$.
$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}\cdot\boldsymbol{n} = 3 - 6 - 8 = -11$, $\lvert\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}\rvert = \sqrt{29}$ and $\lvert\boldsymbol{n}\rvert = \sqrt{14}$.
Write down what you enter, in degree mode: $\sin\theta = \frac{\lvert -11\rvert}{\sqrt{29}\sqrt{14}}$, so $\theta = \arcsin\left(\frac{11}{\sqrt{406}}\right) = 33.0876\ldots^{\circ}$.
Compare: $\arccos\left(\frac{-11}{\sqrt{406}}\right) = 123.0876\ldots^{\circ}$ is the obtuse angle with the normal, and $123.0876\ldots^{\circ} - 90^{\circ}$ gives the same answer.

blocks.text: Using arccos and stopping. That gives the angle with the normal: use arcsin, or subtract from $90^{\circ}$.

blocks.prompt: Find the acute angle between the line $\boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\1\end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and the plane $3y + 4z = 10$.
blocks.hint: The plane has no $x$ term, so its normal is $(0, 3, 4)$.
blocks.explain: $\boldsymbol{b}\cdot\boldsymbol{n} = 0 - 6 + 8 = 2$, $\lvert\boldsymbol{b}\rvert = 3$, $\lvert\boldsymbol{n}\rvert = 5$, so $\sin\theta = \frac{2}{15}$. $82.3^{\circ}$ is the angle with the normal; $21.0^{\circ}$ uses the point instead of the direction.

blocks.prompt: Find the acute angle, in degrees, between the line $\frac{x - 1}{2} = \frac{y}{-2} = \frac{z + 3}{1}$ and the plane $4x + 4y - 7z = 0$. Give your answer to 3 s.f.
blocks.hint: The denominators give the direction, $(2, -2, 1)$. Then use $\sin\theta$, not $\cos\theta$.

blocks.text: Look along the line where two planes meet, so each appears edge-on as a straight line with its [[normal-vector|normal]] at right angles to it. Turn one plane onto the other, and its normal turns by the same angle.

blocks.alt: Two planes seen edge-on as two straight lines crossing at a point, which is their line of intersection seen end-on. Plane 1 is horizontal and plane 2 rises at an angle theta to it. Normal n1 points straight up from plane 1 and normal n2 points out at right angles from plane 2. The angle between the two normals is also marked theta.
blocks.caption: Rotating $\Pi_{1}$ onto $\Pi_{2}$ rotates $\boldsymbol{n}_{1}$ onto $\boldsymbol{n}_{2}$ by the same angle $\theta$.

blocks.statement: The [[angle-between-two-planes|angle between two planes]] is the acute angle $\theta$ between their normals $\boldsymbol{n}_{1}$ and $\boldsymbol{n}_{2}$. It satisfies $\cos\theta = \frac{\lvert\boldsymbol{n}_{1}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}_{2}\rvert}{\lvert\boldsymbol{n}_{1}\rvert\lvert\boldsymbol{n}_{2}\rvert}$.
blocks.plain: How far one plane is tilted from the other.

blocks.text: It is the booklet's formula for the normals, with a modulus, since reversing a normal flips the sign. If $\boldsymbol{n}_{1}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}_{2} = 0$, the planes are perpendicular.

blocks.question: Find the angle between the planes $2x + 2y + z = 4$ and $x + 4y - z = 2$.
steps: Read off the normals: $\boldsymbol{n}_{1} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{n}_{2} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\4\\-1\end{pmatrix}$.
Scalar product: $\boldsymbol{n}_{1}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}_{2} = 2 + 8 - 1 = 9$.
Magnitudes: $\lvert\boldsymbol{n}_{1}\rvert = \sqrt{4 + 4 + 1} = 3$ and $\lvert\boldsymbol{n}_{2}\rvert = \sqrt{1 + 16 + 1} = \sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}$.
So $\cos\theta = \frac{9}{3 \times 3\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.
This is a standard exact value, so $\theta = 45^{\circ}$.

blocks.question: Find the acute angle between the planes $\Pi_{1}: 3x - y + 2z = 5$ and $\Pi_{2}: x + 4y - 3z = 2$. Give your answer in degrees to 3 s.f.
steps: Normals: $\boldsymbol{n}_{1} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{n}_{2} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\4\\-3\end{pmatrix}$.
$\boldsymbol{n}_{1}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}_{2} = 3 - 4 - 6 = -7$, $\lvert\boldsymbol{n}_{1}\rvert = \sqrt{14}$ and $\lvert\boldsymbol{n}_{2}\rvert = \sqrt{26}$.
Without the modulus, $\arccos\left(\frac{-7}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt{26}}\right) = 111.524\ldots^{\circ}$, obtuse because the scalar product is negative.
Write down what you enter, in degree mode: $\theta = \arccos\left(\frac{7}{\sqrt{364}}\right) = 68.4754\ldots^{\circ}$, which is $180^{\circ} - 111.524\ldots^{\circ}$.

blocks.text: Stopping at an obtuse angle. A negative scalar product gives an angle over $90^{\circ}$: take the modulus, or subtract from $180^{\circ}$.

blocks.prompt: The planes $kx + 2y - z = 1$ and $3x - y + 4z = 6$ are perpendicular. Find $k$.
Find the acute angle between the planes $x + 2y + 2z = 1$ and $2x - y - 2z = 7$.
blocks.hint: Both normals have magnitude $3$. Watch the sign of the scalar product.
blocks.explain: $\boldsymbol{n}_{1}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}_{2} = 2 - 2 - 4 = -4$, so $\cos\theta = \frac{4}{9}$ and $\theta \approx 63.6^{\circ}$. $116^{\circ}$ is the obtuse angle; $26.4^{\circ}$ uses sine.

blocks.text: Line meets plane: substitute the general point into the plane and solve for $\lambda$. One value: one point. $0 = 0$: the line lies in the plane. $0 = q \neq 0$: parallel, no meeting.

Two planes with non-parallel normals meet in a line with direction $\boldsymbol{n}_{1} \times \boldsymbol{n}_{2}$. Find a point by setting $z = 0$ (or $x = 0$ or $y = 0$ if the direction's $z$-component is $0$).
Three planes: one solution is a single point; a one-parameter family is a common line (a sheaf); no solution means two parallel planes or a triangular prism.

mistakes: Using arccos when a line meets a plane. That gives the angle with the normal: use arcsin, or subtract from $90^{\circ}$.
Giving an obtuse angle between two planes. Take the modulus of the scalar product, or subtract from $180^{\circ}$.
Concluding that a line lies in a plane from one point. Also show $\boldsymbol{b}\cdot\boldsymbol{n} = 0$.
Setting only the last row's coefficient to zero. A common line also needs a zero right-hand side; otherwise the planes share no point.
Sign slips in a vector product's middle component. Check the result against both normals: each scalar product must be $0$.
Using the normal as the direction of a line parallel to a plane. A parallel line needs $\boldsymbol{b}\cdot\boldsymbol{n} = 0$.
examTips: “Interpret geometrically” wants the arrangement in words: a point, a common line, parallel planes or a prism. Justify it from the normals.
To “show that” a line is parallel to a plane, show $\boldsymbol{b}\cdot\boldsymbol{n} = 0$. To show it is not in the plane, show one of its points is off it.
Paper 1 angles are exact, such as $\sin\theta = \frac{1}{2}$, so $\theta = 30^{\circ}$. On Paper 2, give the acute angle in degrees to 3 s.f.
On Paper 2, write down the expression or augmented matrix you enter before the GDC's answer. That line earns the method mark.
